references.text: Jeremiah warns against the false prophets who speak lies, and the people love it that way. This parallels the warning in Luke 6:26 that false prophets were spoken well of by everyone.

Isaiah describes a people who ask their prophets to speak pleasant things and deception instead of the truth. This illustrates how false prophets became popular because they said what the people wanted to hear.

Micah describes how a prophet who promises wine and strong drink would be accepted by the people. This shows how false prophets became popular and well-liked, just as Jesus warns against in Luke 6:26.
Jesus says that the world loves its own but hates his disciples because they are not of the world. Being spoken well of by everyone can be a sign that one belongs to the world rather than to Christ.
James warns that friendship with the world is enmity against God. This corresponds with the warning that being praised by all people may indicate that one pleases the world rather than God.

John writes about false prophets that they are of the world, and therefore the world speaks their language and listens to them. This is directly parallel to Jesus' woe to those whom everyone speaks well of.

Jesus warns against false prophets who come in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. The theme of false prophets is shared with Luke 6:26, where the fathers' treatment of false prophets is mentioned.

The prophet Micaiah stood alone against 400 false prophets who spoke to please the king. This is an example that the fathers preferred false prophets who said what they wanted to hear, as Jesus refers to in Luke 6:26.

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says that his disciples are blessed when they are persecuted and slandered. The contrast is clear: those who are persecuted for Christ's sake are blessed, while those whom everyone speaks well of receive a woe.
